key_terms.meaning: Motion where the restoring force is proportional to displacement and opposite to it: F = −kx; the result is a sine or cosine in time.
ω = 2π/T = 2πf = √(k/m), measured in rad/s; it sets how fast the phase of the oscillation advances.
T = 2π√(m/k) for a mass–spring system; it depends on mass and stiffness only, not on amplitude.
The angle in x = A sin(ωt + φ) that fixes where the oscillator was at t = 0; it is set by initial conditions, not by the system.
For a wire of radius r, length l and modulus of rigidity η: C = πηr⁴/(2l), in N m per radian.
T = 2π√(I/C), where I is the moment of inertia of the suspended disc about the wire axis and C is the couple per unit twist.
I = Σmr² for a body about the axis of rotation, in kg m²; for a disc of mass M and radius R, I = ½MR².
A velocity-opposing force F = −bv, with b the damping coefficient in kg/s; it removes mechanical energy from the oscillator.
ω′ = √(ω₀² − b²/4m²), slightly below the natural frequency ω₀ = √(k/m).
Q = ω₀m/b = ω₀/Δω, where Δω is the width of the resonance peak; a large Q means a sharp, slowly decaying resonance.
The condition where the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, giving maximum amplitude of a forced oscillator.
∂²y/∂x² = (1/v²) ∂²y/∂t² for displacement y travelling along x with speed v.
v = √(T/μ), with T the tension in newtons and μ the linear mass density in kg/m.
At any point the net displacement is the algebraic sum of the displacements due to each wave separately.
The pattern formed by two equal waves travelling in opposite directions; points of zero amplitude are nodes and of maximum amplitude are antinodes.
Average power crossing unit area, I = ½ρvω²A² for a mechanical wave; it grows with the square of amplitude and of frequency.
L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) decibels, with reference intensity I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m².
The time for the sound energy density in a room to fall to one-millionth of its steady value, that is, a 60 dB drop.
The property of certain crystals such as quartz to develop a voltage when pressed, and to change shape when a voltage is applied.
A crystal of thickness t resonates at f = v/(2t), where v is the speed of the longitudinal wave in the crystal; this sets the ultrasound frequency.
A set of equally spaced obstacles or slits that diffract sound; maxima occur at d sin θ = nλ, with d the grating element spacing and n = 0, 1, 2, …
A longitudinal sound wave of frequency above about 20 kHz, beyond the hearing range of humans.

takeaways: In SHM the restoring force is proportional to displacement, so the motion is sinusoidal and the period is fixed by mass and stiffness alone.
A torsional pendulum is the rotational twin of a mass–spring system, with torque −Cθ replacing force −kx and moment of inertia replacing mass.
Damping makes the amplitude decay exponentially and slightly lowers the frequency; a periodic drive can pump energy back in.
Resonance is the large response that occurs when the drive frequency is close to the natural frequency, and the quality factor measures its sharpness.
The wave equation links the curvature in space to the acceleration in time; for a string the speed follows from tension and mass per unit length.
A travelling wave transports energy proportional to A² and ω², while a standing wave stores energy and transports none on average.
Sound is a longitudinal pressure wave, and the decibel scale is logarithmic because the ear responds to ratios, not to absolute intensities.
Room acoustics is decided by absorption: too little gives a long reverberation, too much gives a dead, muffled sound.
A piezoelectric crystal converts an alternating voltage into mechanical vibration, and it radiates most strongly at its thickness resonance, well above 20 kHz.
Ultrasonics works because short wavelengths travel in narrow beams and reflect sharply from boundaries, which is the basis of echo ranging, testing and cleaning.
bank_note: Long answers are usually derivations plus applications: the wave equation for a stretched string and the resulting v = √(T/μ), the torsional pendulum period, piezoelectric production of ultrasonics with the acoustic grating equation, and the uses of ultrasound.

bank.q: Define simple harmonic motion. Starting from F = −kx, derive the expression for the displacement and the time period of a mass–spring oscillator, and explain why the period does not depend on amplitude.
outline: Define SHM by the force law F = −kx
Write a = −(k/m)x and identify ω² = k/m
Solve to get x = A sin(ωt + φ)
Obtain T = 2π√(m/k)
Explain that ω contains only k and m, so amplitude cancels out

bank.q: What is the couple per unit twist of a wire? Derive C = πηr⁴/(2l) by considering a cylindrical shell inside the twisted wire, and hence obtain the period of a torsional pendulum.
outline: Define C as the torque needed for unit twist
Take a shell of radius x, thickness dx and find its twist angle
Use shear modulus η to get the restoring torque on the shell
Integrate from 0 to r to get C = πηr⁴/(2l)
Write τ = −Cθ and compare with F = −kx
Conclude T = 2π√(I/C)

bank.q: Describe damped harmonic motion. Write the equation of motion with a damping force −bv and discuss the over-damped, critically damped and under-damped cases.
outline: Equation m d²x/dt² + b dx/dt + kx = 0
Amplitude decays as e^(−bt/2m)
Damped frequency ω′ = √(ω₀² − b²/4m²)
Over-damped: slow non-oscillatory return
Critically damped: fastest return without oscillation
Under-damped: decaying oscillation

bank.q: Explain forced oscillations and resonance. Draw the amplitude versus driving-frequency curve for different damping values and define the quality factor.
outline: Driven equation with F₀ cos ωt
Steady amplitude depends on ω and b
Peak near ω = ω₀, exactly at √(ω₀² − b²/2m) for amplitude
Smaller damping gives taller, narrower peak
Define Q = ω₀/Δω and state its meaning
One example: tuning a radio, or a bridge responding to marching

bank.q: Define intensity of sound and intensity level in decibels. Explain reverberation time and absorption coefficient, and state the factors that control the acoustics of a hall.
outline: I = power per unit area, W/m²
L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀) dB with I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m²
Sketch of a 10 dB rise meaning ten times the intensity
Define reverberation time as a 60 dB decay
Define absorption coefficient as fraction of energy absorbed
Mention volume, surface area, audience and open windows as controls

bank.q: A 200 g block hangs from a spring of stiffness 80 N/m. Find the angular frequency, the time period, and the maximum speed if the amplitude is 5 cm.
outline: State units at every step

bank.q: A disc of moment of inertia 2 × 10⁻⁴ kg m² is suspended from a wire whose couple per unit twist is 8 × 10⁻³ N m/rad. Find the period of torsional oscillation.
outline: T = 2π√(I/C)
Substitute I and C with units

bank.q: A string of linear mass density 0.01 kg/m is stretched by a tension of 90 N and fixed at both ends 1 m apart. Find the wave speed, the fundamental frequency, and the frequency of the second harmonic.
outline: Fundamental: λ = 2L, so f₁ = v/2L = 47.4 Hz
Second harmonic f₂ = 2f₁ = 94.9 Hz
Note that the antinode count goes up by one each time

bank.q: The intensity level of one sound is 70 dB and of another is 40 dB. Find the ratio of their intensities and the difference in level.
outline: L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀)
Difference = 30 dB
30 = 10 log₁₀(I₁/I₂), so I₁/I₂ = 10³
Explain that 30 dB means a thousand times more intensity

bank.q: A quartz crystal of thickness 1 mm is used to produce ultrasound. Taking the longitudinal wave speed in quartz as 5760 m/s, find the fundamental thickness-resonance frequency and say whether it lies in the ultrasonic range.
outline: λ/2 = t, so λ = 2 mm
This is far above 20 kHz, so it is ultrasonic
Mention that higher harmonics appear at odd multiples

bank.q: In an acoustic grating experiment a parallel beam of sound of frequency 40 kHz falls on a grating of element spacing 2 cm. Find the wavelength and the first-order diffraction angle.
outline: Take v ≈ 340 m/s in air
d sin θ = nλ with n = 1

bank.q: Derive the wave equation for transverse waves on a stretched string by considering the net vertical force on a small element, and hence show that the wave speed is v = √(T/μ). State the assumptions made.
outline: Take an element of length dx and mass μ dx
Net transverse force from the difference of tension components
For small slope, sin θ ≈ tan θ = ∂y/∂x
Net force = T(∂²y/∂x²)dx
Apply Newton's second law with mass μ dx
Get ∂²y/∂x² = (μ/T) ∂²y/∂t²
Compare with standard form to read v = √(T/μ)
Assumptions: small amplitude, uniform string, no damping, tension unchanged

bank.q: Explain the formation of standing waves on a string fixed at both ends. Derive the positions of nodes and antinodes and the allowed frequencies, and compare the energy transport in a standing wave with that in a travelling wave.
outline: Superpose y₁ = A sin(ωt − kx) and y₂ = A sin(ωt + kx)
Result y = 2A sin kx cos ωt
Nodes where sin kx = 0, that is x = nλ/2
Antinodes midway between nodes
Boundary condition y = 0 at both ends gives L = nλ/2
f_n = nv/2L, giving the harmonic series
Travelling wave carries power P = ½μvω²A²; standing wave carries zero average power but stores energy between nodes

bank.q: Describe the piezoelectric method of producing ultrasonics. Explain the role of the thickness resonance, compare it briefly with the magnetostriction method, and state two applications of ultrasonics that depend on its short wavelength.
outline: Quartz or Rochelle salt or PZT slice between metal plates
Alternating voltage from a valve or transistor oscillator
Crystal changes dimensions at the driving frequency
Resonance when t = λ/2, giving f = v/2t
Piezoelectric: high frequency up to MHz, stable, small output; magnetostriction: lower frequency, larger power, needs nickel core
Applications: echo ranging needs narrow beams; non-destructive testing needs small flaws to be resolved
Also mention cleaning by cavitation

bank.q: Explain, with the resonance curve of a forced oscillator, why soldiers break step on a bridge and why a car suspension is deliberately damped. Relate the discussion to the quality factor.
outline: Driven amplitude peaks near natural frequency
Marching supplies a periodic force at a fixed frequency
If that frequency matches the bridge frequency, amplitude grows until failure
Breaking step spreads the driving frequencies
Suspension uses damping to flatten the peak and stop repeated bouncing
Large Q means a sharp peak, small Q a flat one
Design chooses Q to suit the job

glossary.def: A repeated to-and-fro motion about a fixed mean position.
The force that pulls an oscillator back towards its mean position, proportional to displacement in SHM.
The maximum displacement of an oscillator or a wave from its mean position.
The time taken for one complete oscillation, measured in seconds.
The number of oscillations per second, f = 1/T, measured in hertz.
ω = 2πf, the rate at which the phase of an oscillation changes, in rad/s.
The quantity (ωt + φ) that specifies the state of the oscillator at time t.
Oscillation in which the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement and directed opposite to it.
A disc or bar suspended by a wire, oscillating by twisting and untwisting the wire.
The torque required to twist a wire by one radian; C = πηr⁴/(2l).
The ratio of shear stress to shear strain in a material, denoted η or G, in N/m².
The rotational equivalent of mass, I = Σmr², in kg m².
The progressive loss of energy from an oscillating system, usually to friction or viscous drag.
The constant b in the damping force F = −bv, in kg/s.
The large-amplitude response that occurs when the driving frequency approaches the natural frequency.
A dimensionless measure of how sharp a resonance is, Q = ω₀/Δω.
The partial differential equation whose solutions are travelling or standing waves of speed v.
Mass per unit length of a string, μ, in kg/m.
The rule that displacements from separate waves add algebraically at every point.
A wave pattern with fixed nodes and antinodes, formed by two identical waves travelling in opposite directions.
A point in a standing wave where the displacement is always zero.
Wave power crossing unit area perpendicular to the direction of travel, in W/m².
A logarithmic unit for comparing two powers or intensities, one bel being a ratio of ten.
The time for sound in an enclosure to decay by 60 dB after the source stops.
The production of a voltage by mechanical stress on certain crystals, and the reverse change of shape under voltage.
The formation and violent collapse of tiny vapour bubbles in a liquid under intense ultrasound.
A periodic array of obstacles or slits that diffracts sound waves into orders given by d sin θ = nλ.
A longitudinal sound wave with frequency above about 20 kHz, inaudible to humans.
